Justin Gonzalez Datasheet as part of Automatic Pet Feeder for Team 206

Submission: December, 07, 2026

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: • This is a breakdown of our teams sensing bowl. The primary function of this board is to monitor the amount of food is in the bowl and to communicate to the other boards with a digital signal when to release more food into the bowl and when to stop.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text:
• Our team is trying to offer a reliable solution for pet owners to feed their furry friends when they are away. Our goal is to create an autonomous system that is able to know when the bowl of food needs to be refilled and can fill up in the absence of the owner ensuring that their pet have access to food throughout the day. For more context on the team's development process see to the link below to have access to the teams report which will also have links to the other team member's websites for a deeper look into all of the boards.
  • team report.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The block diagram below demonstrates the measuring and control subsystem for Team 206's pet feeder. It shows the connections between the three light sensors, push buttons, LEDs, curoisty nano board, power supply, and team interface, including signal types, voltagle levels and pin assignment.

docs.title: Power Source
docs.text: The subsystem is powered from 9 V, 3 A unregulated supply. The 9V supply feeds a voltage regulator that provides a regulated 5 V output for the subsystem.

docs.title: Power Levels
docs.text: The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano and MCP6004 op-amp operate using the regulated 5V supply. The photoresistor voltage dividers, push-button circuits, and LEDs also operate within the 0-5V range. The 9V supply provides the input to the 5V voltage regulator.

docs.title: Sensors
docs.text: Each photoresistor forms a voltage divider that produces an analog signal. The signal is filtered and buffered using an MCP6004 op-amp configured as a voltage follower before being read by the PIC18F57Q43 ADC

docs.title: Actuators/ Outputs
docs.text: Two LEDS provide visual indication of the selected fill level. The microcontroller also provides digital output signal to the motor subsystem when filling should begin or stop based on the selected level and sensor reading.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text:
Table 1: Op Amp

Solution Pros Cons * Option 1.* MCP6004-I/P Quad Operational Amplifier* $0.60/each*Link to product * Operates on 5V* Four amplifiers in one* Low supply current (100 μA per amplifier)* Rail-to-rail inputs and outputs * Maximum Supply Voltage 6V needs regulation from 9V power source * Lower bandwidth (1 MHz) than the TL974IN (12 MHz)*Input offset voltage can introduce small measurements errors * Option 2. * TL974IN Quad Operational Amplifier * $1.66/each * Link to product * Works with 5V supply* Four amplifiers in one * Higher bandwidth(12 MHz) * More expensive * Higher power consumption *Limited input common mode voltage range * Option 3. * LM324N Quad Operational Amplifier * $0.58/each * Link to product * Operates on 5V* Four amplifiers in one * Inexpensive * Not rail-to-rail * Input common-mode range does not extend to the positive 5V supply rail *Higher input bias current (45nA) than the MCP6004 (1pA)

Choice: Option 1: MCP6004-I/P Quad Operational Amplifier

Rationale: The MCP6004 was selected becuase it can operate a 5V power supply and will have four Op Amps in one chip, which is enough for the three light sensors in our design. Its rail-to-rail input and output capability allows it to work with sinals close to the supply voltage. It also has low power consumption and is less expensive than option two.

Table 2: Light Sensor

Solution Pros Cons * Option 1.* PDV-P8103 CdS Photoresistor * $0.72/each*Link to product * Inexpensive* High dark resistance (500 kOhms minimum)* Resistance changes with light exposure * Requires a voltage-divider circuit * Lower minimum dark resistance than option 2*Ambient Lighting may affect readings * Option 2. * NSL-A95013 CdS Photoresistor * $0.88/each * Link to product * High minimum dark resistance (1.2 MOhms)* Resistance changes with light exposure * Good at detecting blocked light * More expensive than Option 1* requires a voltage divider circuit *Ambient lighting may affect readings * Option 3. * Adafruit 161 CdS Photoresistor * $0.95/each * Link to product * Simple design* Through hole installation * Detects changes in light when sensor is blocked * Most Expensive* Low Minimum dark resistance (200 kOhms) *Light resistance is not listed

Choice: Option 1: PDV-P8103 Photoresistor

Rationale: Option 1 was selected because of changing resistance when exposed to light allowing the system to detect when food blocks light at different levels of the container. It is affordable, uses through-hole mounting, and can be incorporated into a voltage divider circuit. Since our project uses three light sensors, its lower cost is also beneficial. I will also have access to these in the classroom so if I need spares or replacements.

Table 3: Voltage Regulator

Solution Pros Cons * Option 1.* NJM7805FA 5V Linear Voltage Regulator * $1.85/each*Link to product * Fixed 5V Output * Supports up to 1.5A * Through Hole Mounting * Most expensive*Lower maximum operating temperature (85 °C) *Less energy efficient than a switching regulator * Option 2. * MC7805ACTG 5V Linear Voltage Regultor * $1.07/each * Link to product * Fixed 5V output* Built-in overtemperature and short-circuit protection * Operating temperature up to 125°C *Lower rated output current (1A) * Produces heat when reducing 9V to 5V *Requires external capacitors for recommended operation * Option 3. * L7805ABV-DG 5V Linear Voltage Regulator * $1.53/each * Link to product * Fixed 5V output* Supports up to 1.5A * Overtemperature and short-circuit protection * More expensive than option 2* Produces heat when reducing 9V to 5V *Requires external capacitors for recommended operation

Choice: Option 3: L7805ABV-DG 5V Linear Voltage Regulator

Rationale: Option 3 provides a regulated 5V output needed for the circuit while accepting the 9V input from the power adapter. It includes overtemperature and short-circuit protection. Its 1.5A output rating matches our planned power requirements, provided the circuit's total current consumption stays within the limit

Table 4: 9V Power Supply

Solution Pros Cons * Option 1.* Adafruit 1448 Adjustable Power Adapter* $14.95/each*Link to product * Adjustable output voltage, including 9V * Include multiple connector tips * Can change between center-positive and center negative polarity * Most Expensive*Only supplies 900 mA at 9V,below the 1A requirment *Requires a different jack or connector adapter * Option 2. * GlobTek WR9HD1000LCP-F(R6B) * $10.35/each * Link to product * Fixed 9V output* Provides 1A output current * Less expensive than option 1 *5.5 x 2.5 mm plug does not match the PJ-102AH jack * Not adjustable to other voltages *Requires a different jack or connector adapter * Option 3. * BestCH 9V 3.0A AC Adapter for EDAC EA10302 EDACPOWER 9VDC 3A 3000mA Switching Mode * $4.52/each * Link to product * Fixed 9V output* Rated up to 3A * Most affordable option * Longterm reliability unknown* No datasheet available with this vendor

Choice: Option 3: BestCH 9V 3A AC Adapter

Rationale: The power adapter provides the required 9V and 3A output at a lower cost than the adjustable alternative. It also uses a North American wall plug. Connector Compatibility will be verified before final assembly, and a compatible power jack can be selected if necessary. This is also similar to the adapter distrbted in class which is the one I intend on using.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic represents the light sensor system for our automatic pet feeder. The design uses a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller to monitor three photoresistors that detect different food levels. An MCP6004 operational amplifier(op-amps) buffers the sensor signal before they reach the microcontroller. There are also two push-button switches for selecting the desired fill level, two indicator LEDs, and an output that will be sent to the motor board and tell it when to activate and when to stop adding food. The board can be powered using a 9V DC input with a voltage regulator which will be regulated to 5V or an external regulated 5V supply. There are also additional GPIO connections for testing and potential troubleshooting. The design includes two alternative 8-contact ribbon cable connectors to provide an alternative connection option to J3. And because only one digital signal is needed pins 3 and 5 are just alternate pins available on J3 in case there is issues with pin 4. Also included will be spare GPIO connections where there will be headers in case I run into issues with sensors GPIO's. The LED's and pushbuttons can also be utilized for debugging.

Figure 1: Automated Pet Feeder Light Sensor Schematic

docs.title: Power Budget Calculations
docs.text:
• Curiosity Nano: 13.8 × (5/3) + 0.82 = 23.8 mA. Estimated MCU and ADC current; actual 5V board consumption should be verified.
  • MCP6004 Op-Amp: 0.17 mA × 4 = 0.68 mA. Includes all four amplifiers.
  • Sensor Dividers: [5V ÷ (0.12 kΩ + 10 kΩ)] × 3 = 1.48 mA. All three photoresistors in direct light.
  • Buttons: (5V ÷ 10 kΩ) × 2 = 1.0 mA. Both pressed.
  • LEDs: (5 − 3.0)/1 kΩ + (5 − 2.1)/1 kΩ = 4.9 mA. Both on.
  • J3 Signal Lines: [5V ÷ (330 Ω + 10 kΩ)] × 3 = 1.45 mA. All three high; motor and driver are in the teammate's budget.
  • Total 5V Current: 23.8 + 0.68 + 1.48 + 1.0 + 4.9 + 1.45 = 33.33 mA. Estimated load.
  • 25% Safety Margin: 33.33 × 1.25 = 41.67 mA. Allowance for variations.
  • 9V Supply Current: 41.67 + 6 = 47.67 mA. Includes assumed maximum 7805 quiescent current.
  • Regulator Heat: (9 − 5) × 0.04167 + 9 × 0.006 = 0.22 W. About 11°C rise at an assumed 50°C/W junction-to-ambient thermal resistance.
  • Regulator Headroom: 9 − 5 = 4V. Above the assumed 2V dropout requirement.
  • Battery Comparison: 600 mAh ÷ 47.67 mA = 12.6 hours. Idealized estimate; wall power selected for continuous operation. Power Configuration: The 9V/3A adapter feeds the L7805ABV regulator, which supplies the 5V rail for the Curiosity Nano and PCB components. The 1A fuse provides fault protection.
